content.p: Kyle Bickham was 29 years old and, his family said, on his way home from an overnight shift at Amazon when he boarded a northbound Red Line train on Chicago's South Side on Labor Day, 7 September 2026. Somewhere near the 69th Street station he was forced out of the moving train through its sliding doors. He landed on the electrified third rail and was struck by a train travelling in the opposite direction.

Chicago police first reported that a person had jumped from the train, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. Within days the account changed. Police said three people had pushed him, and prosecutors later said there were four. By 1 October, four people stood charged with first-degree murder: a 19-year-old woman, an 18-year-old man and two 15-year-olds. None has been convicted. Everything below about what happened on the train is the prosecutors' account, given at detention hearings, and only one defence lawyer has so far answered it in public.
content.h2: The man who rode the Red Line
content.p: Bickham's family described him to ABC7 Chicago as the youngest boy among four siblings, a son, brother, grandson and friend. His father, Christopher Bickham Sr., said he loved writing poetry and loved his nieces, and could change the mood of a room just by walking into it. His mother, Latanya Bickham, said he had recently moved into a new apartment and put up with a long commute and an overnight schedule while trying to build a future. His father told another outlet that Bickham had been working since the age of 15.

His grandmother, Bertha Ford, said he kept in touch even when he had no phone, finding a way to call and tell her he loved her. CWB Chicago reported that he had been delivering packages for Amazon; the family spoke of an overnight shift at the company, and the Unheard Voices magazine, citing CBS Chicago, called it a warehouse shift. His family said he had no connection to the people involved in the confrontation, and prosecutors, according to CBS Chicago, said none of the accused knew him.
content.h2: What prosecutors say happened on the train
content.p: The fullest account came from a prosecutors' proffer at McBounds's detention hearing on 23 September, reported by CBS Chicago and FOX 32 Chicago, and from the hearing for Katlar Parchman on 19 September. It rests largely on CTA surveillance video, footage from other passengers and witness statements.

Prosecutors said Parchman, McBounds, a 15-year-old girl and a man who had not been charged all left a bus and reached the 95th Street terminal. Parchman and McBounds paid with Ventra cards; the girl and the man went through the turnstiles without paying. All four sat in one car, and so did Bickham. He sat across from Parchman and began talking with her.

According to prosecutors, Bickham then got up and wandered around the car. He approached a man and said something that could not be made out while looking at the man's bag, and the man told him to get away from it. The defence, at Parchman's hearing, went further: her public defender, Cruz Rodriguez, said the victim was the one who caused trouble, handling riders' purses and smelling of alcohol. Prosecutors at the same hearing also said he seemed intoxicated and was handling belongings. Prosecutors said that at one stop Bickham stepped off and then reboarded.

A couple of minutes later, prosecutors said, he began arguing with the 15-year-old girl, and the two moved around the car shouting at each other. At some point he spat at the girl, and the spit also struck Parchman. Prosecutors said one of the men then grabbed Bickham by the arm while the girl punched him in the face. Several outlets reported that Parchman, the girl and the two men then surrounded him and began punching him as the group moved toward the end of the car; one man began to choke him, and others pulled at his head.

Prosecutors described a short lull near the sliding doors, during which Bickham stooped to retrieve his headphones. The two men then forced him into the corner by the doors while the two women closed in, according to prosecutors. They said one of the men pulled the emergency lever with the train in motion, and the doors slid open. The girl stepped up beside him and, as Bickham resisted, grabbed him by the head and shoulder and heaved him out, prosecutors said, with Parchman and McBounds standing right next to them. Chicago police have said he landed on the third rail, where he lay until another train struck him moments later.

Prosecutors said witnesses heard someone say "He shouldn't have bothered us" before leaving the train at a later stop. Outlets disagree on who the speaker was: CBS Chicago and FOX 32 Chicago attributed it to the girl, while NBC Chicago and CWB Chicago reported that the witnesses heard Parchman say it.

Prosecutors said all four were identified through surveillance video. For Parchman, prosecutors said, the Ventra card she used at 95th Street was linked to her name and phone number. They also said investigators found an Instagram story posted from her account on the day, with a selfie in the same clothes she wore in the footage, and that a witness picked her out of a photo array.

Parchman was arrested on 16 September on North Keeler Avenue. Prosecutors said that after she was read her rights she spoke to detectives and identified herself, the girl and the two men in still images from the CTA footage. They said she told detectives she slapped Bickham three or four times after he spat on her and then stopped. Detectives searched her phone with her consent and found searches for "good places to lay low" and "who are the police looking for" after the attack, prosecutors said.

McBounds was identified through his own Ventra card, prosecutors said. Investigators contacted the college he attends and learned that he stopped going to classes on the day Bickham died. A warrant was issued, and he was arrested at his home in Morgan Park. Prosecutors said he had no criminal record.

The 15-year-old girl was the first to be charged. Police said detectives arrested her on 11 September, and at her first juvenile court appearance a judge kept her in custody. She faces five felony charges, including murder, aggravated battery and mob action. Because she is a minor she has not been named.

Parchman, 19, of Garfield Park, was charged on Friday 18 September with first-degree murder, aggravated battery and mob action, among other felonies. At her first court appearance, on Saturday 19 September, Assistant State's Attorney Marilyn Salas told Judge Deidre Dyer that Parchman was one of four people who physically attacked Bickham and then pushed him out of the train. The state alleged that she punched and grabbed him and pulled at his head. Salas said the defendant "acted in concert with" three other people. Rodriguez said there was no indication she was the person who actually pushed Bickham out. The judge ordered her held until trial and issued an order preserving video taken aboard the train. A report carried by Yahoo News said Parchman is a state-registered certified nursing assistant with a past in home health care, and has no prior criminal history.

McBounds, 18, was charged with first-degree murder, two further counts of murder committed during another forcible felony, aggravated battery of a transit employee or passenger, and mob action. A Cook County judge denied him pretrial release on Wednesday 23 September, and he was due back in court on 7 October.

The last defendant is a 15-year-old boy. The Sun-Times reported that he was arrested on a Tuesday; FOX 32 Chicago said Wednesday, in Englewood on the South Side. A police source told CBS Chicago the charges were filed that Wednesday. A police source told CBS Chicago he faces one count of first-degree murder, two of felony murder, one of mob action and one of aggravated battery of a transit employee or passenger. Prosecutors had long said one of the four was a man at large, and CBS Chicago reported that prosecutors said the boy and the girl together pulled the emergency lever, opened the doors and pushed Bickham out. Earlier prosecutors' accounts had the lever pulled by one of the men and the girl pushing with help from a man. Police have not said whether the four will be tried together, FOX 32 Chicago reported. The boy is not named because of his age.

Relatives gathered at the 69th Street station on a Sunday and asked for witnesses and the remaining suspects to come forward. His brother asked those involved to surrender. Latanya Bickham asked what security riders have once they step on a platform, and the family questioned the lack of security on the train. ABC7 Chicago reported that the CTA did not immediately respond to a request for comment about those concerns. A fundraiser started by relatives was collecting money for funeral costs.

Bickham's father told ABC7 that he wanted justice and closure. After Parchman's arrest he said he hoped his son's attackers would "get right with God," adding that they had taken something precious from his family and from the world.

Hoodline, summarising Sun-Times reporting, put the killing against a transit system whose figures were moving in different directions. Overall crime on the CTA fell 30 percent in the first half of the year after stepped-up patrols by police and the Cook County sheriff's office from March, and the Red Line saw a 47 percent fall in all crime and a 76 percent fall in violent crime through June, compared with the year before. That followed a record 469 violent attacks on the system in 2025, the most in more than 25 years, according to the same reporting. The Sun-Times also noted that Bickham's death was the ninth homicide of the long Labor Day weekend.

Each of the four defendants is presumed innocent, and no court has yet tested the prosecutors' narrative. The defence has already suggested a different picture of the victim's behaviour, and Parchman's lawyer said there was no indication she was the person who pushed him. The accounts also differ in small ways: police gave the time as about 2:40 p.m., while the account at the Parchman hearing gave around 2:30 p.m., and the early police statement of three attackers gave way to four. The roles of the girl, the boy and the two men, and who pulled the lever, are described differently across the reports as the cases were filed.
